The typical subspecies, subsp. ebracteatus, is represented by the extra-Australian distribution apart from its occurrence in the mangroves of Escape River in north Queensland (Duke 2006).

ecology_description: Some initial observations were made on the pollination strategies of Acanthus ilicifolius by Primack et al. (1981). Flowers of Queensland plants are adapted for cross-pollination rather than self-pollination, although the latter can occur. While pollen is present from opening of the flower, the stigma does not become receptive until the flower has been open for a full day. The pollinator (Yellow-breasted Sunbirds, and probably Xylocopa bees) in probing for nectar at the base of the flower, separates the two pairs of stamens, allowing the stigma to descend and pick up previously deposited pollen from its back. When the pollinator withdraws from the flower the anthers come together again and pollen is deposited on its back. Duke (2006) also suggested that the chief pollinators in Australia are the bees. Aluri et al. (2017) also investigated the pollination of A. ilicifolius in India, indicating that flowers were visited by Xylocopa and blue-banded (Amegilla cingulata) bees, a wasp species (Odynerus sp.) and a butterfly species (Borbo cinnara); all of these genera occur in Australia. In keeping with the findings of Primack et al. (1981), their study confirmed that pollination was most effective when carried out by bees. Fruits take about a month to mature and, as with many Acanthaceae species, are flung out when the capsule explodes in response drying. They can be dispersed up to 2 m and can presumably be further dispersed by tidal movements. They germinate in the wet season (Aluri et al. 2017). After clearing of mangroves in India, Acanthus ilicifolius becomes dominant (Aluri et al. 2017) forming large patches by both vegetative means and from seed.
habitat_description: Part of the mangrove association of northern Australia. Duke (2006) indicates that Acanthus ilicifolius occupies an intermediate upstream estuarine position where salinity is less than sea water but not affected by freshwater, and its inundation frequency from tides varies from high to low indicating that it is tolerant of inundation from less than 20 times per month to more than 45 times per month. They can form "dense frontal thickets" or exist as patches in the understory up to the high water margin.
distribution_description: Acanthus ilicifolius is a mangrove species found from India, throughout Malesia extending to the Solomon Islands, New Hebrides and New Caledonia. It has apparently been introduced into South Africa (Clarke 1912). In Australia it is found along the tropical coastlines in saline tidal areas from the Daly River in the Northern Territory east to the Fitzroy River in Queensland (Duke 2006).
seedling_description: Cotyledons c. 14--21 × 18--21 mm, rather thick and fleshy, base auriculate. First pair of leaves with toothed or smooth margins. At the tenth leaf stage: leaf margin armed with spines or pungent points. Stems clothed with purple, slightly raised glands. Seed germination time 27 to 41 days.
notes: The majority of Australian populations of Acanthus ilicifolius have been collected with toothed leaves and axillary spines, but specimens with entire leaves and lacking axillary spines do occur. Spinyness of the leaves is generally attributed to increased exposure to the sun (Duke 2006, Ragavan et al. 2015), but this too is in need of further study.

distribution_description: A native southern European and northern African species, but because of its use in horticulture it is now regarded as an introduction in the Americas, South Africa and New Zealand. Acanthus mollis was introduced to Australia as a garden plant and has become naturalised at least in the eastern states and southeastern South Australia and southwestern Western Australia, where it is likely that because of its ability to reproduce from root fragments it has persisted in areas which were formerly gardens. Once present it can be extremely difficult to eradicate.
notes: Acanthus mollis is an environmental weed in parts of Australia as well as the rest of the world, e.g. see Weeds of Australia Acanthus mollis fact sheet and A. mollis in Global Invasive Species Database http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/species.phpsc=1663#. In this second sheet, written in 2010, it is stated that A. mollis is listed in the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Poisonous Plant Database but if that was the case it is no longer listed as so. While some populations never seem to form fruit, as in the author's garden, others are extremely fertile.

biostatus: Naturalised; listed weed in some jurisdictions. In N.S.W. there is a 'general biosecurity duty' to prevent, eliminate or minimise any biosecurity risk posed by subsp. micrantha, as well as a 'N.S.W. Control Order' in which owners and occupiers of land on which there is subsp. micrantha must notify the local control authority for the area of its presence, destroy all subsp. micrantha present and keep the land free of it (NSW WeedWise 2019). It has been included on the National Environmental Alert List for weeds in Australia (as Asystasia gangetica subsp. micrantha) since 2000.

ecology_description: Chinese Violet plants spread by seed and plant fragments, and can flower and fruit year round. The seeds are dispersed explosively from the drying fruit capsules. After most of the ripe capsules have released their seeds, the plant dies back to ground level. Winter frosts kill above-ground plant parts but plants regrow the following spring from their basal shoots. Trailing stems can take root at each node when they come into contact with moist soil. Most infestations in Australia have occurred as a result of dumping garden waste or uncontrolled garden plantings growing into nearby areas.
habitat_description: Recorded from a wide range of habitats in its native Africa, but when introduced, often associated with plantations or disturbed areas. In Australia known from waste areas often in sandy coastal areas.
distribution_description: Asystasia gangetica subsp. micrantha is native to tropical Africa and Arabia, as well as South Africa, Madagascar and the Mascarene Islands. It has been introduced relatively recently into Asia where it is recorded from Malaysia, Singapore and China as well as Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Australia. It was first brought to attention in Australia in New South Wales from Boat Harbour, north of Newcastle in 1999. The taxon is presently known from disjunct localities in the Gold Coast and Shoalwater Bay areas in Queensland and from Rapid Creek in Darwin in the Northern Territory (Skinner 2015, Westaway et al. 2016); also recorded for Christmas Island, viz. Lepschi 6448 (CANB).

dispersal_description: This is not surprising - during summer months, when Avicennia seeds are dispersing, a strong warm ocean current (the Leeuwin Current) runs south along the Western Australian coastline, across the Great Australian Bight to South Australia then south to Tasmania (see Fox, Flora of Australia 1: 211 (1999) & Walker, Flora of Australia 1: 423 (1999)) It would be surprising if this current did not carry a regular supply of sea-dispersed seeds from Western Australia to South Australia (but not Victoria) In this treatment, the South Australian populations are treated as subsp. marina, although it is acknowledged that they may also carry some genetic influence of subsp. australasica, transported on the Flinders Current northwestwards from Victoria
habitat_description: Found on intertidal mudflats. Tolerant of tidal seawater inundation, as well as occurring in brackish waters in the upper reaches of riverine estuaries. Often forming monotypic forests or shrubberies of large extent.
distribution_description: Found throughout the margins of the Indian Ocean and Red Sea, Malesia and Western Australia, extending to the gulfs and peninsulas of South Australia. In Australia, recorded from about Bunbury to Joseph Bonaparte Gulf in Western Australia. and from Ceduna/Nuyts Archipelago to near Adelaide in St Vincent Gulf in South Australia.
notes: According to Duke (1991) this taxon is confined, in Australia, to the Western Australian coast between Bunbury and about Broome. Present observations extend the range of subsp. marina northwards to Joseph Bonaparte Gulf. More importantly, most South Australian material more closely matches subsp. marina than subsp. australasica (sepals with a broad glabrous margin, style extending only to base of anthers) although in bark characters there seems some influence of subsp. australasica. This is not surprising - during summer months, when Avicennia seeds are dispersing, a strong warm ocean current (the Leeuwin Current) runs south along the Western Australian coastline, across the Great Australian Bight to South Australia then south to Tasmania (see Fox, Flora of Australia 1: 211 (1999) & Walker, Flora of Australia 1: 423 (1999)). It would be surprising if this current did not carry a regular supply of sea-dispersed seeds from Western Australia to South Australia (but not Victoria). In this treatment, the South Australian populations are treated as subsp. marina, although it is acknowledged that they may also carry some genetic influence of subsp. australasica, transported on the Flinders Current northwestwards from Victoria.

distribution_description: Native to Asia including China, India, Laos, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Vietnam. Currently, Barleria cristata has a pantropical distribution and can be found naturalised in Africa, North America, Central America, the West Indies and on islands in the Pacific Ocean (CABI 2020). In Australia it has been recorded as a garden escape in northern Queensland and in the Northern Territory in Darwin. Although it is known to be present in the Kimberley gardens it has not yet been recorded as naturalised there or elsewhere Western Australia. Barleria cristata has the potential to spread much further in tropical areas because of its ability to sucker easily. Also introduced to Christmas Island.
notes: Some accounts of Barleria cristata (Backer & Bakhuizen van den Brink 1965, Cramer 1998) indicate that capsules are not formed but this does not appear to be the case in Australia. For instance, in the population on Darnley Island (B.M. Waterhouse 7745 & S.G. McKenna) the infestation is described as including seedlings, and other specimens record plants as spreading by seed from a neighbouring block (Cowie 12696). On the Darnley Island collection (B.M. Waterhouse 7745 & S.G. McKenna ), it is noted that the Queensland Health nurse had commented that B. cristata caused her skin to itch when she cut it back. Barker in Barker & Telford (1993: 381, 383) provides a treatment for Barleria cristata on Christmas Island.

distribution_description: Native throughout the tropics of Africa and Asia if the broad Brummitt & Wood (1983) classification is accepted (see Taxonomic notes), but confined to India under the concepts of Darbyshire et al. (2010, 2015, 2019) and therefore a weed in most tropical areas of the world. In Australia, Barleria prionitis was originally recorded from the Northern Territory from a vacant block in Darwin and from the Victoria River Downs Station area in the 1960s, probably from discarded pot plants. A population from waste places on the Ross River in Townsville, Queensland, has apparently now been eradicated, but the Victoria River Downs plants are still persistent, though under “active control” (pers. comm. 2004, B.M. Waterhouse, NAQS). Andrew Mitchell (pers. comm., 24 May 2002) indicated that B. prionitis had escaped into a creek at Argyll Diamonds in E. Kimberley, Western Australia, but there are no herbarium specimens (AVH, accessed 15 August 2019) to confirm this. A specimen from Boigu Island in Torres Strait collected in 2001 (Waterhouse 6239) referred to a small naturalised population persisting on a sand spit from dumped garden plants. Plants were collected again from this site in March 2004 (Waterhouse 6804) with comments about its spread since the original collection, and in 2012 it was again collected (S.G. McKenna 1224) from the same site where it had been previously controlled.

They may germinate from where they land or be further dispersed by water, animals and in mud. The seeds are covered with hygroscopic hairs which expand on wetting and then attach the seed to the surface on drying. Dumped garden waste and roadside slashing both aid in dispersal of the species.

distribution_description: An introduced species, native to South Africa; naturalised in Hawaii (Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER) 2017). In Queensland there are existing collections from the Cairns and Cooktown areas, from the Mackay and Gladstone areas (see Weedspotters Newsletter March 2007) and the Brisbane City council area. It is also a weed on Magnetic Island but there is no herbarium specimen (Simpson 2018). In northern New South Wales it has been recorded from the Taree-Forster area and from the Lake Macquarie area. Keighery & Keighery (2025) recorded B. repens as an escape due to garden refuse dumping in Tuart woodland near Joondalup, a northern suburb of Perth. A photograph sent for identification to the PERTH herbarium resulted in quick identification and B. repens was eradicated from the area. A collection has been deposited in the WA Herbarium but has yet to appear in AVH records.
notes: The presence of curved hardened processes at the nodes may have a role in helping this plant to spread. These processes, which appear to be hardened bracts or bracteoles, could be confused with spines and they are presumably the means by which the plant is able to scramble over other vegetation. The Nursery & Garden Industry, Queensland, produced a Grow Me Instead booklet for the Dry Tropics in 2009. Instead of planting B. repens, which produces seed and is also capable of rooting from the nodes, they promoted the growing of Barleria obtusa “Purple Gem” since it was not an invasive threat. While this may be true if that particular cultivar does not produce seed, the image shown on the website was not a Barleria but a Pseuderanthemum cultivar, probably P. atropurpureum variegatum. Plants for sale under the name Barleria “Purple Gem” have been seen similarly mislabelled at a nursery and at Bunnings in Palmerston. Barleria repens was the subject of a weed alert in March 2010 (Technigrow 2010).

distribution_description: Native to the Indian subcontinent and recorded by Hu et al. (2011) for Bhutan, Cambodia, Yunnan in China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Vietnam but in some of these cases e.g. Java (Backer & Backhuizen van der Brink 1965) they represent cultivated records. In Australia it occurs as an escaped garden plant in north Queensland, presently found in the Cooktown to Cairns area with a single record from Sarina.
notes: Barleria strigosa was first collected by Ernie Stephens, a member of the North Queensland Naturalists Club, and a colleague of Hugo Flecker, in 1949. The plant was not collected again until 1987 from the government research station at Kamerunga near Cairns. Since 1995 there have been a number of collections from the Cairns area and some of these have been outside gardens. It has certainly spread into the Cairns Central Swamp, a sink for a whole lot of garden escapes and has been collected several times in the Cooktown area since 1998 (pers. comm. J. Clarkson, 26 May 2009). In 2000 it was recorded as naturalised on the hillside adjacent the Cooktown Botanic Gardens (B.M. Waterhouse 5950).

ecology_description: Brillantaisia lamium spreads by seeds and by layering. The long capsules each produce about 30 seeds and these are flung out of the capsule when it explodes in response to wetting or drying. The seeds are covered with hairs that in the dry state are pressed to the surface, but on wetting these expand and exude a mucilage which probably glues the seed to a surface as it dries again. As with other Acanthaceae species, all nodes are capable of forming roots and so any stem fragments or sprawling plants are capable of taking root (Barker 2007). It can disperse further than the local area by water and as contaminant of vehicles, machinery and nursery stock (Grice & Setter 2003).
habitat_description: Brillantaisia lamium's preference is for wetter and shaded areas where it will eventually form dense mats of vegetation because of its sprawling habit. In Australia it has been found growing along the edges of waterways, in orchards, in nurseries and around sugarcane plantations and it is able to grow in shade. Where there is plentiful moisture it has the potential to invade disturbed areas such as roadsides, agricultural clearings and gaps in forests. It is a known troublesome weed forming dense stands beneath tropical African crops such as coffee, oil-palm, bananas and rubber.
distribution_description: Brillantaisia lamium is native to wet forest regions of Africa, from Sierra Leone on the west coast to Ethiopia, almost on the eastern coast and then south to Tanzania and northern Angola. It has naturalised in Kenya and is quite capable of forming weedy populations in cleared areas or in plantations in areas where it is native (Sidwell 1998). In Australia it was first collected from the Innisfail area in northern Queensland in 1996 but is now also known from Alexandra Bay near Daintree and from rainforest margins at Whyanbeel Creek, where, in 2000, it was described as a common weed. It was recorded from the Brisbane area at Toowong in late 2005. It most likely originated as a garden escape since a number of species are known in the garden trade.
seedling_description: Cotyledons semi-orbicular, c. 8--10 × 13--16 mm, 3-veined but venation difficult to see, base truncate, apex obtuse to emarginate. First pair of true leaves opposite, ovate, upper and lower surfaces clothed in hairs, midrib raised on the upper surface. At the tenth leaf stage: leaf blade ovate to lanceolate, base attenuate, both the upper and lower surfaces clothed in hairs. Petioles c. 30--40 mm long, upper half winged. Stem distinctly 4-angled and glabrous except near the base of the petioles.
notes: Fears are held that thius species may become a serious weed of the Australian tropics and it is listed as a Sleeper Weed, Category 4, on the Australian Government's Weeds in Australia site. See also Brillantaisia lamium in Brisbane City Council weed identification tool (accessed 27 September 2019).

Crayn 466 et al., NSW) | tube 3--4.4 mm long | throat 9--10 mm long | lobes 5--7.5 mm | Filaments glabrous | Ovary with 6 superposed ovules per cell | style c. 7.5 mm long, pubescent above | stigma unequally lobed

habitat_description: In Queensland, all collections are from along watercourses in complex notophyll vineforest or closed rainforest or from sides of tracks, suggesting that the species requires good light. In New South Wales found on meta-sediments in riparian rainforest; also wet sclerophyll forest.
distribution_description: South-eastern Queensland in coastal areas north of Brisbane, from Upper Tallebudgera, south of Brisbane and from Dalrymple Heights near Mackay. More recently collected from far north-eastern New South Wales.

common_name: Fire-cracker Plant or Firecracker Flower, a reference to the capsules which explode and disperse the seeds when water is applied; also Candlestick Plant, a reference to the long, upright inflorescence.
flowering_time_description: Flowers c. spring-summer ; flowers recorded October, , December, February, March

ecology_description: Populations of Crossandra infundibuliformis from areas in the Whitsunday Shire, Queensland, produce seed and other specimens also have seeds present in older inflorescences (A report to the Whitsunday Pest Management Committee by Peter Alden, Land Management Officer, Whitsunday Shire Council, 14 March 2006). It has been scored as producing viable seed in Hawaii, where it has also been scored as being self-compatible or apomictic (Crossandra infundibuliformis HEAR.ORG record sheet, 2010). This may be because cultivars are involved.
habitat_description: Recorded as naturalised in rainforest around Cairns (viz. R.L. Jago & B. Wannan 4201, BRI). Also spreading from ornamental plantings in gardens.
distribution_description: Native of India, Sri Lanka, Nepal. In Australia, sparingly naturalised in Queensland.
notes: The cultivar 'Fireglow', with vibrant orange flowers set against glossy green leaves was bred for increased drought tolerance as well as better colour. 'Fireglow' grows to a height of c. 25--40 cm and has deep orange blooms that last well into spring and autumn. (Gardening Australia Fact Sheets: New Releases, ser. 16, episode 34, 2005; Firecracker Flower Plant Profile, ser. 33, episode 25, 2022). Simpson (2018) also provides information about cultivars on his website.

flowering_time_description: Flowering variable, probably dependent on rainfall, February-September

distribution_description: Found in the north-western region of Western Australia, in areas peripheral to the Hamersley Ranges.

habitat_description: Usually associated with watercourses, D. glabra has been recorded from mixed shrubland with Callitris on shale, from Acacia citrinoviridis woodland with an understorey of Corchorus and Cymbopogon in the cobble bed of a creek, and also as growing on scree on the lower slopes of hills.
distribution_description: Known only by a few collections from iron rich alluvial soil in Wittenoom Gorge and Robe River which are both in the Fortescue River watershed of the Pilbara region of north-western Western Australia.

flowering_time_description: Flowers March-July, with occasional records outside this period
breeding_system_description: Dicliptera armata produces both showy and cleistogamous flowers.

pollination_description: Dicliptera armata produces both showy and cleistogamous flowers
habitat_description: A woodland understory species usually found at the edges of creeks and rivers, where it is often extremely abundant.
distribution_description: Endemic Australian species common throughout northern tropical Australia. Noticeable in its distribution is its absence from Cape York Peninsula, where D. ciliata and D. spicata both occur, a disjunct population at Millstream in Western Australia, and a single disjunct collection from east Arnhem Land, Northern Territory (Westaway 3992, CANB, DNA).
notes: Dicliptera armata produces both showy and cleistogamous flowers.

flowering_time_description: Flowers May-June, with collections later than this date usually fruiting only

seed_description: Seeds smooth
phenology_text: Flowers May-June, with collections later than this date usually fruiting only.
habitat_description: Grows in sandy or loamy soil in Allosyncarpia forest and at the base of the rocks of the escarpment in the Kakadu area; in areas outside Kakadu it is still usually recorded as coming from river banks or from sand amongst sandstone outcrops with Eucalyptus and Triodia.
distribution_description: Known from Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory but there are also a few collections from further south from the Roper River and the McArthur River.
notes: Dicliptera arnhemica appears to produce only showy flowers.

biostatus: By its collection from Goulbourn Island in 1818 the species has always been assumed to be native. However, this is such a localised occurrence it is quite possible that it represents a pre-European introduction.
habit_description: Decumbent, spreading herb to 30 cm high

fruit_description: Capsule glandular-hairy apically, 2-seeded
seed_description: Seeds smooth
habitat_description: The only note on a collection: "occurs in gravelly soil within woodland" (Munir 6172).
distribution_description: First collected from the Goulbourn Islands off the coast of Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory by Alan Cunningham in 1818, while on the first of Phillip Parker King's surveys of the Australian coastline. It was not collected again until the 1980s and even since then collections have been few. One collection (Munir 6172) came from the adjacent mainland southeast of Murgenella.

common_name: Chinese Foldwing, Double Folding Wing Plant.

One Australian record is from a moist, shady location on a creek bank at high water level where it covered an area of 1 square m.
distribution_description: Native to China, SE Asia, India and Pakistan. Sparingly naturalised in Brisbane and Caloundra in SE Queensland.

biostatus: Native? It may be that Dicliptera ciliata is an introduction to Australia since there appear to be no herbarium specimens dated earlier than 1880.

seed_description: Seed barbed-tuberculate all over
habitat_description: Found in vine thicket or as an understory in monsoon woodland. On Cocos (Keeling) Islands, grows in forest under Pisonia grandis and in Cocos plantations in coralline sand Barker & Telford (1993: 386--387).
distribution_description: In Australia it is found in the Kimberley region of Western Australia, Alligator River area of Northern Territory and islands and coastal rivers of Cape York Peninsula in Queensland. Outside Australia found in Timor and New Guinea, possibly also occurring in Java and the Philippines, even as far as India and China, but because of doubts about which name to apply to this species (see Barker 1986) the extent of its distribution is uncertain.

distribution_description: At the time of publication in 1986, Dicliptera miscella was known only by collections from Careening Bay and Augustus Island, both coastal localities in the Bonaparte Archipelago of northwestern Western Australia. Since then, there have only been two further collections, another from Careening Bay in 1993 (Stewart 9261) and one more recently from further north than the rest of the collections, from Vansittart Bay in the east Kimberleys in 2018 (Leach 4825).
notes: Appears to produce both cleistogamous and chasmogamous flowers.

habitat_description: Recorded as being from along creek banks associated with vine forest, sometimes on steep slopes.
distribution_description: In Australia, Dicliptera spicata collections come from Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, and Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory. There are two outliers on the Australasian Virtual Herbarium map (accessed 25 August 2020), one from a crusher vine thicket in monsoon forest from a non-specified locality in the Kimberleys (Hyland 16501) and another from Westmoreland Station in the Gulf of Carpentaria (Thompson 954); neither of these specimens have been seen by the author and are in need of checking. Dicliptera spicata also occurs in Timor, which is part of the Lesser Sunda Islands, and it may occur on some of these islands as well, but it is otherwise unknown in Malesia. As with Dicliptera ciliata, which also occurs in Timor and the Lesser Sunda Islands, there are apparently no herbarium colllections of the species from Australia which are dated before 1880, raising the possibility that this is an introduced species. Both species are predominantly from coastal localities.

flower_description: Calyx 7--8.5 mm long, finely eglandular-hairy internally and on margins | Corolla white to pale yellow or creamy-white | tube 20--26 mm long | throat 9.5--17 mm long, hairy externally, glabrous internally | lobes 7.5--8.5 mm long, spreading | Stamens exserted | filaments glabrous | Ovary glabrous except for sparse glandular hairs apically | style hairy, c. 3--3.5 cm long

seed_description: Seed c. 3.5 mm diam
pollination_description: Since the flowers open at night and are spent by very early morning and possess an extremely long tube with exserted stamens and stigma, it is likely that they are moth-pollinated Cleistogamous flowers, indicated by shorter styles (c. 1 cm long), may also be produced in this species
ecology_description: Since the flowers open at night and are spent by very early morning and possess an extremely long tube with exserted stamens and stigma, it is likely that they are moth-pollinated. Cleistogamous flowers, indicated by shorter styles (c. 1 cm long), may also be produced in this species. Food plant for moths and butterflies. Dipteracanthus bracteatus has been documented as a food plant for the larvae of the butterfly Yoma sabina (Australian Lurcher, The Lurcher) (Braby et al. 2018, Herbison-Evans & Crossley 2016, Vane-Wright & de Jong 2003: 211). The Common Eggfly (Hypolimnas bolina) is also listed for this species and other species of Acanthaceae in north-eastern Queensland (Anon. undated).
habitat_description: Recorded from rocky slopes within Eucalyptus forest or woodland, from the edge of a mangrove-paperbark forest, from cattle paddocks of partially cleared Corymbia/Melaleuca woodland burned a few months previously (Waterhouse 8034) or as an "occasional plants straggling through dense Heteropogon contortus/Cenchrus elymoides grassland" (Waterhouse 5082). Soils recorded include clay, granitic, lateritic and red loam. There are records of it growing within garden beds (McKenna 560) and in an Asian herb garden on a cultivated plain (Mitchell 8688), and it is possibly difficult to remove in such situations as Waterhouse comments on several of her collections on it being "firmly rooted" in the soil, probably because of its thickened roots.
distribution_description: In Australia known only from Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, adjacent Torres Strait islands and Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory; also occurs in New Guinea.

flowering_time_description: The only flowering material recorded has been in March after good rains and so it seems likely that flowering will be sporadic and dependent on rainfall as it is in Ruellia primulacea
habit_description: Spreading, glabrescent, perennial subshrub to 30 cm high, with short-lived, quadrangular stems from a perennial rootstock
stem_description: Older stems with light grey bark | young stems light green or grey-green, the two opposite faces shallowly grooved (the grooved faces alternating at the nodes)
leaf_description: Leaves petiolate | lamina elliptic to ovate, 15--25 (-38) mm long, 7--10 (-28) mm wide | base tapering | margin entire | somewhat undulate | apex acute to less commonly obtuse | midrib raised on both surfaces | lateral veins ascending | the lower three pairs subopposite or alternate, the remainder alternate | surface very sparsely hairy to sparsely pubescent above, sparsely pubescent below | the hairs to 2 mm long, not scabrid | cystoliths present on both surfaces, randomly oriented | petiole 1--2.4 mm long, deeply to shallowly concave above, convex below | the lamina narrow-elliptic, 6.5--12.3 mm long, glabrous to very sparsely hairy above, sparsely pubescent below | petiole 0.7--1.3 mm long, glabrescent

phenology_text: The only flowering material recorded has been in March after good rains and so it seems likely that flowering will be sporadic and dependent on rainfall as it is in Ruellia primulacea.
habitat_description: Collections of D. chichesterensis are "from areas of red-brown cracking clay soils associated with basalts on the Chichester Plateau. The collections are from a variety of landforms on the plateau, including slopes, tablelands, benches and creek margins" and usualy from "Acacia xiphophylla tall shrublands" with an understory ofTriodia wiseana.
distribution_description: Known only from five locations on the Chichester Range in the Pilbara region of Western Australia.

distribution_description: Recorded from Africa, Arabian Peninsula, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, southern Malesia to the Pacific (New Caledonia, Vanuatu, Samoa, Hawaii); it has probably been introduced in SE Asia since first records are usually after 1900. In Australia, herbarium specimens would indicate that the plant has increasingly been recorded since 2000 from islands in the Torres Strait, a number of townships on Cape York Peninsula e.g. Weipa, Coen and from Cooktown to Cairns, Queensland, from suburbs associated with Darwin and Palmerston in the Northern Territory, and from a homestead in the Kununurra region in the Kimberleys, Western Australia. Mention of a sighting in Barron Gorge by the Cairns SGAP group in 2019 (Jago & Worboys 2019) indicates that it is spreading outside more urban areas. There are also records of the species from Christmas and Norfolk Islands.

habitat_description: In its natural state Graptophyllum excelsum has usually been recorded as having been found in pockets of soil derived from weathered limestone, among the rocks and crevices on steep, rough, eroded hillsides in semi-evergreen vine thicket. More recent collections would indicate a wider soil preference and also give more indications of species associations. For instance, the Fell collection from the Cooktown region was recorded as coming from a "deciduous vine thicket with scattered emergents of Bombax ceiba var. leiocarpum, Gyrocarpus americanus, Brachychiton sp. and Garuga floribunda emergents and a canopy of Drypetes deplanchei, Croton arnhemicus, Canarium australianum, Cocholospermum gillivraei, Dinosperma erythrococcum, Sersalisia sericea, Paraserianthes toona, Aidia racemosa, Schefflera actinophylla, Alphitonia excelsa and Melia azedarach. Granite pavement and boulder field... Common in understorey". The W.J. McDonald 5684 & R. Melzer collection from the Shoalwater Bay training area was from a "Rocky footslope, clay loam soil, volcanic soil, in complex notophyll vine forest with Argyrodendron trifoliolatum, Bosistoa medicinalis, Strychnos axillaris and Archidendropsis thozetiana prominent. Abundant at this site". The collection by Ward (Ward 820) from Jimna represents the most southerly record of G. excelsum. Here it was recorded from a Hoop Pine scrub edge and was considered by locals to be native because it was so common, but there remains the possibility that it is an introduction at that site.

distribution_description: Graptophyllum pictum is cultivated throughout the world, usually as the 'Caricature Plant'. New Guinea has been proposed as the home of G. pictum and here it has been recorded from logged-over forest and rainforest undergrowth as a tree but it is also often grown as an ornamental or as a hedge plant around villages. Smith (1991) suggests introduction to the Pacific may have been by first peoples. In Australia it is known only by a single scrappy collection from Murray Island in Torres Straits, Queensland.
notes: While Linnaeus attributed the type to Asia in the protologue Lindley (1829) commented on how common it was in cultivation in gardens throughout the whole of India, and it having a local name, but its native country was unknown. However it was referred to in the text accompanying the plate as the East Indian Caricature plant, perhaps suggesting an Indonesian origin. Suggestions for G. pictum being native in New Guinea are primarily based on this being the only place known where it forms fruits (Barker 1986). Both Fosberg et al. (1993) and Daniel (2000) have questioned this suggested place of origin for the domesticated plants since these differ both morphologically and in their chromosome numbers from natural habitat collections from New Guinea. Fosberg suggested that it might be native in the Moluccas. The type of the species in the Linnean Herbarium lacks any coloured areas on the leaf. The pollen is heterocolpate; see apsa.anu.edu.au/family/ACANTHACEAE/genus/Graptophyllum/sample/271--5-/image/equatorial%20vieworder=asc&sort=spec

ecology_description: Following clearing of part of the Buderim population in the early 2000s many G. reticulatum plants resprouted, and fruit and prolific flowering were observed (Shapcott 2000, Lynch 2007). Graptophyllum reticulatum is a slow-growing shrub with a juvenile period estimated at over two years and a lifespan of over 30 years. It regenerates through resprouting and possibly from a short-lived seed bank. Viable seed has only been recorded by Shapcott (2000) while MacIntyre (in Lynch 2007) indicated that those seeds which were produced tended to be eaten and bored into by insects. While there is little recruitment from seed in the wild, garden-grown species of Graptophyllum, such as G. ilicifolium, can produce dozens of self-sown seedlings each year (I. Champion, pers. comm. in Lynch 2007). The population genetics of Queensland’s Graptophyllum species were investigated by Dr A. Shapcott, University of the Sunshine Coast (Shapcott 2005), who found: (i) All four species have quite high levels of genetic diversity, although G. reticulatum has the lowest diversity. (ii) All species were significantly inbred but G. reticulatum was the most inbred. (iii) Genetic differentiation between populations was highest in G. reticulatum. (iv) The Buderim population of G. reticulatum population had higher genetic diversity than the other populations. (v) Genetic diversity appears to be correlated with population size. (vi) Gene flow between populations of G. reticulatum is low enough to cause population divergence and loss of allelic diversity due to genetic drift. (vii) The Dulong Road BCR population and the Buderim population are more similar genetically than either to the Triunia National Park population, despite the geographic proximity of the Dulong and Triunia sites.
habitat_description: Restricted to lowland subtropical rainforest, particularly in complex notophyll vine forest mixed with tall to very tall closed forest and riparian rainforest. Grows in creek-lines and gullies on the upper slopes of olivine basalt caps, near the edge of escarpments. The species is also known to occur in disturbed areas with rainforest or pasture and Acacia melanoxylon regrowth adjacent to complex notophyll vine forest (Lynch 2007).
distribution_description: Endemic to south-eastern Queensland, being restricted to the Maroochy Shire Council local government area. Two populations are located close together in the Nambour district, while a third occurs on the eastern slopes of Mt Buderim, farther east on the Sunshine Coast. All three populations occur within remnant rainforest patches, c. 15 km apart (Misiak 1998); two of these occur on protected land. Estimates of the total population size of G. reticulatum vary, ranging between 800--1500 individuals (Lynch 2007). There were 16 or 17 collections in herbaria (AVH, accessed 24 February 2020).
notes: Woody capsule fruits are rarely seen (Bean & Sharpe 1991) and were not reported from field observations until 2000 (Shapcott 2000).

ecology_description: While mostly growing submerged, Hygrophila polysperma is emergent in shallow water and can form dense floating mats. It prefers flowing water but tolerates slower moving water (NSW WeedWise 2018). Submerged leaves are larger than those which are not submerged. While it does form seed it is not known whether this contributes to the plants spread. Its main means of dispersal is by broken stem fragments. An article by Cuda & Sutton (2000) considers many of the attributes of Hygrophila polysperma which made it a successful weed species after its introduction to Florida, U.S.A. as an aquarium plant.
habitat_description: Freshwater lakes, ponds and dams, apparently able to grow in water up to 3 m deep (NSW Weedwise 2018).
distribution_description: A native of parts of China and the Indian subcontinent. Naturalised in tropical parts of the U.S.A. and also the Mediterranean. First collected in Australia in 2005. It is recorded from Eltham and from Tea Gardens and the Tweed and Clarence Rivers in northern New South Wales, and from Caboolture River and Ennogera Creek in south-eastern Queensland, not all of these with herbarium vouchers. A recent specimen from Babinda in northern Queensland requires confirmation since it is sterile.
notes: This species has the potential to become a serious weed of freshwater lakes, ponds and dams in eastern Australia. It prefers flowing water in warmer environments, but may also be found in slow moving waters and lakes. East Indian Hygrophila (Hygrophila polysperma) is a fast growing invasive plant that out-competes native aquatic plants while the dense mats of floating vegetation that it forms are able to obstruct waterways and shade out submerged plants. It can occupy the entire water column and also creates problems as an emergent plant along the margins of waterbodies. (Weeds of Australia - Biosecurity Queensland Edition 2016: https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/hygrophila_polysperma.htm). A weed risk assessment (Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk) reveals that it is a weed of high risk.

ecology_description: The crowded inflorescences of Hypoestes aristata mean that at any one time there are usually a large number of flowers with their associated nectar and pollen available, and studies in Africa (Padyšáková et al. 2013) have documented 15 different visitors ranging from sunbirds to various insect representatives. Individual flowers last up to five days and during this time they produce nectar which accumulates in the narrow, c. 1 cm long corolla tube. The lilac-purple flowers with their paler-coloured nectar guide at the base of the upper lip and their exserted style and stamens would suggest insect pollination and two carpenter bee species (Xylocopa spp.) were found to be the most effective pollinators, leading to seed formation, while none of the other visitors were of the right size to achieve this and were basically nectar robbers. This latter category included the sunbirds and the honeybees. Further observations by the same group (Tropek et al. 2013) indicated that where there were large populations of H. aristata flowers the sunbirds would prevent the carpenter bees from accessing them, thus protecting their nectar source. In Australia the cultivated H. aristata appears to be self-pollinating. In the author's garden copious seed is formed without any apparent pollinator being present. Two bird species, the New Holland Honeyeater and the Eastern Spinebill have been seen visiting flowers, as have occasional Honey Bees, but these are likely to be seeking nectar.

Most records seem to have arisen from pot plants “gone wild” and so care should be taken when growing the species in proximity to native vegetation. distribution_description: A common species found throughout northern Australia. Regional studies of the past have produced various numbers of species for the genus but the most recent global treatment by Daniel & McDade (2014), including both morphological and molecular work, supports a single variable species with the possibility of a second in Africa. Outside Australia the species is native to Asia and Africa while its occurrence in the Americas may be a mixture of older and more recent introductions. Vollesen (2008) strongly disagreed with the single species concept as proposed by Hossain (1984), indicating at least three species in Africa, and an endemic species in both South America and Australia.

ecology_description: The red flowers of Odontonema cuspidatum attract honey-eaters and sunbirds in northern Queensland at least (Odontonema tubaeforme in Discover Nature at JCU, undated, accessed 2020), but whether they are effective pollinators or just robbers of the nectar at the base of the tube is not known. Nor is it known whether fruits are produced and whether seed is also a factor in the spread of this plant. As with many Acanthaceae species they may be effectively spread by vegetative means alone. Comments on this species in the Tropical Garden Society of Sydney indicate that seeds are not produced and it spreads by suckering but this may only apply to more southerly occurrences. A comparative study of nectar-robbing of this species by stingless bees in semi-natural habitat and a coffee plantation in Mexico (Fitch & Vandermeer 2021) is useful for insights into its reproductive biology. Weed risk assessments (Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk 2008; CABI 2020) give this species a high score and cover some of the reproductive biology as part of their attributes scores, but some of the information surrounding seed set may not apply in Australia. Butterflies are also mentioned as visitors to the flowers.

habitat_description: Both the Bean and Batianoff collections record the species from disturbed forest or woodland areas near waterways. For instance, the Bean collection, (BRI AQ15241), records the species as being “common on loamy soil in a disturbed open forest near creek, with Eucalyptus siderophloia and Lophostemon confertus...” while the Batianoff collection, (BRI AQ200901), records it as “occasional on the bank of the Brisbane River in clay soil in a Eucalyptus tereticornis woodland with lantana & garden plants escapees”.
distribution_description: Native to Bhutan, India, Nepal. Naturalised in the Brisbane area, Queensland, since at least 1999. One old record from New South Wales in the 1800s (Moore s.n., MEL) was almost certainly a cultivated plant since Charles Moore was the director of the Sydney Botanic Gardens from 1848 to 1896 and exchanged collections with Mueller.
notes: In establishing the requirement of P. speciosa as a potted plant, Grueneberg (1998) indicated that P. speciosa could be propagated "by seeds (germinated after 10 days) and also by cuttings (7 cm long, rooted after 18 days) and that this was easy at any time of the year. This ease of reproduction no doubt contributed to a high weed risk assessment for Hawaii (Chimera 2019).

notes: Pseuderanthemum tenellum is variable in the extent of hair covering on the outside of the corolla tube, on the style and on the fruits. Flowers are sometimes of two different sizes on the one shrub at maturity and measurements given in the description are for larger flowers. Larger flowers appear to be homostylous since the style develops to the top of the tube (c. 9--11 mm long) and hence the stigma is at a similar height to the mature anthers. Smaller flowers have tubes 4--7 mm long and lobes c. 3 mm long; they are not cleistogamous as in P. variabile, but heterostylous. In the shorter-tubed flowers the style is either very short (c. 0.5 mm long) or exceeding the anthers by up to 2 mm (see for example, Forster 7850). The number of flowers preserved on specimens is usually small and field work is needed both to confirm these observations and to understand the contribution of these different flower types to the biology and variation of the species. There is at least one record (Phillips 1737, n.v.) of P. tenellum in which the label data indicates its occurrence in the same locality as P. variabile in dry rainforest.

ecology_description: Frequently found after bushfires of the previous year. The diversity of ecological habitats probably account for the polymorphism of the species. Pseuderanthemum variabile is recorded as a hostplant for the caterpillars of the Leafwing Butterfly (Doleschallia bisaltide), Blue-banded Eggfly (Hypolimnas alimena), Danaid Eggfly (Hypolimnas misippus), Blue Argus (Junonia orithya) and the Common Eggfly (Hypolimnas bolina) in north-eastern Queensland (Anon., undated). Jordan & Schwenke (2005) list P. variabile as one of the Top 10 butterfly plants for SE Queensland. Braby & Westaway (2021) also list P. variabile as one of few natural food plants for the Blue-banded Eggfly (Hypolimnas alimena darwinensis) in the Darwin region. Flower sprays are eaten by Bearded Dragon Lizards: http://www.saveourwaterwaysnow.com.au/01_cms/details.aspviewMode=printable&ID=388
habitat_description: Occurs in a variety of ecological habitats such as vine forest, rainforest, brigalow (Acacia harpophylla) scrubs, frontal dunes in Casuarina woodland and open forest country and on a diversity of soil types ranging from soils derived from granite to sandstone.
distribution_description: Found in the northern part of Northern Territory, throughout Queensland and along the eastern coast of New South Wales, to just north of the Victorian border; also extends into New Guinea and New Caledonia.
seedling_description: Cotyledons almost orbicular, c. 5--6 mm diam. First pair of leaves opposite, ovate or elliptic, sparsely hairy. At the tenth leaf stage: leaves lanceolate, apex acute, base attenuate, petiole long and slender. Leaf lamina sparsely clothed in short hairs. Roots rather thick, pale coloured. Seed germination time 16 days.
notes: Cleistogamous flowers are often found in Pseuderanthemum variable. The terminal inflorescences usually have showy flowers while the cleistogamous flowers are more often found in the axillary clusters. Their presence is indicated by very short styles (much shorter than usual) at the apex of the developing capsule. Heterostyly does not appear to be exhibited by P. variabile but this needs to be confirmed with field observations. Pseuderanthemum variabile can become a nuisance and one Victorian orchid nursery complains of its presence within their collections suggesting that it is often spread within pots of Dendrobium they receive from northern Australia (Australian Orchid Nursery 2020). The rhizomatous root makes it difficult to remove. It is likewise reported as a weed of shade in Houston, Texas, but is not considered to be invasive (Herself's Plants (undated)).

habitat_description: A rarely encountered species found in gullies or on rocky mesas with shallow infertile soils, frequently common where it occurs. Usually associated with Gidgee (Acacia cambagei) or Wilga (Geijera parviflora). Silcock (2014) classified Rhaphidospora bonneyana as a residual endemic species adapted to isolated residual habitat, in this case "Tertiary sandstone ranges (encompassing mesas, slopes, plateaux, toeslopes), and low hills and gibber plains of the Channel Country" of SW Queensland, with naturally few populations and a relatively restricted range.
distribution_description: From south-western Queensland and far north-western New South Wales, although presumed extinct in the latter state since it is only represented there by the original Bonney collections of the 1870s. A relatively recent collection (Silcock JLS1345) from near the N.S.W./Qld border indicated that it does still exist further south of the main distribution; this collection was made following two wetter than average years and despite some plants being grazed by goats and wallaroos, Silcock recorded that there were ungrazed plants, that flowers and fruits were present and that there were several populations. A collection by Forster (Forster 22296) in 1998 from the Vindex Range in Bladensburg National Park, Queensland, represents a disjunct northern occurrence and here the species was recorded as common.

ecology_description: Sanchezia parvibracteata reproduces vegetatively, with broken fragments easily taking root. It also suckers profusely and can form dense thickets under rainforest edges, especially along creeks and other damp, low-lying areas (Queensland Department of Agriculture & Fisheries 2020). Cultivated material is often without fruits overseas but at least one Australian herbarium collection (Gray 6423, n.v.) records their presence, and so seed may also contribute to naturalisation. Most naturalisations are associated with abandoned gardens or abandoned garden waste. In their South American distribution, S. parvibracteata flowers are visited by hummingbirds (Wasshousen & Wood 2004).
habitat_description: Sanchezia parvibracteata has become an environment weed in places. It often forms dense covers in the understory of native and secondary rainforests where it out-competes native plant species (CABI 2020). In Australia S. parvibracteata usually grows in shade in disturbed areas of lowland rainforest and also in the understory of intact rainforest as well as along creek banks (Zich et al. 2020).
distribution_description: While probably native to Brazil, Columbia, Peru and Ecuador in South America, Sanchezia parvibracteata is widely cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions of the world. It is now naturalised in a number of areas including Costa Rica in central America and Hawaii and New Caledonia in the Pacific Ocean. In Australia it is naturalised in the Babinda and Palmerston areas of NE Queensland.

In Australia recorded from herbarium specimens as occurring in "mesophyll rainforest with Calamus, Pandanus monticola, Terminalia, Syzygium, plus weedy sedges" (Bean 18705), from "riparian woodland of Casuarina cunninghamiana, Ficus virens var. sublanceolata with Syzygium australe, Lantana and Megathyrsus below" (McKenna 90), prolific in a regenerating rainforest (Bean 26769), on a roadside in rainforest (Phillips 1156) and in complex mesophyll rainforest (Jago 7610).
distribution_description: Native from Eastern Himalayas to northern Thailand and south-western China. Widely cultivated in tropical countries and naturalised in Java, Malaysia and Sri Lanka, as well as La Reunion, Mauritius and Jamaica (Meyer & Lavergne 2004). In Australia naturalised in north-eastern Queensland at higher localities in the hinterland, south of Cairns.
notes: Cultivated plants and plants of cultivated origin seem always to be glabrous, pink-flowered and sterile with dispersal being by cuttings or shoots broken off by grazing animals. This species is occasionally confused with Strobilanthes cusia (Nees) Kuntze (syn S. flaccidifolia) in cultivation since it is also known as the Chinese Rain Bell. Strobilanthes cusia is an important dye plant in Vietnam and adjacent areas and is also used for its medicinal properties (Strobilanthes cusia (PROSEA) 2016).

Moylan et al. (2002) record it as occurring in cultivated places in the Philippines.

It has been widely cultivated under the name Thunbergia fragrans and is now considered to be naturalised in the Americas, Africa and the Indo-Pacific as well as in Queensland in Australia.

This means it must not be released into the environment unless the distribution or disposal is authorised in a regulation or under a permit. Move to appropriate place.

Documentation of its introduction to areas around the world can be seen in CABI (2019). In Australia, naturalised in Queensland where it often smothers native vegetation as well as pastures in the Cairns area; also in the Northern Territory and doubtfully naturalised on Norfolk Island.
notes: Cyathiform glands appear as black dots on the surface of the rachis, pedicels and bracteoles. It is proposed that these extra-floral nectaries attract ants which then deter other insects from attacking the plants.

ecology_description: The flowers produce large amounts of nectar and are visited by hummingbirds in Connecticut, U.S.A. (Thunbergia mysorensis in Plant Biodiversity Conservatory and Research Core, accessed January 2024).
habitat_description: Usually found around towns or on old settlement sites, which may suggest persistence rather than new plants. Since the species does not usually form fruits in cultivation, new plants are from cuttings or layering of the stem. The few specimens in herbaria, not seen by me, often indicate an inability to distinguish whether the plant concerned has escaped or is a remnant of cultivation, e.g. the McKenna collection from a "mixed cultivated land and roadside vine forest remnant" where the vine has achieved 10 m in height in the rainforest canopy and forms a "dense hanging curtain". It is clearly a plant that should not be planted near rainforest margins because of its ability to spread in this way.
distribution_description: Native of southern India in the Mysore region, commonly cultivated in tropical areas. Cultivated as an ornamental in Queensland with some apparent escapes in the Cairns, Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast areas.
notes: Scored as being a low risk of becoming weedy in the Pacific (PIER 2005): http://www.hear.org/Pier/wra/pacific/thunbergia_mysorensis_htmlwra.htm The woody base, the source of numerous long runners, is recorded as 4 cm diameter with a nondescript outer surface on the Gray 20334V (QRS) specimen (see image in Gallery). Notes with this specimen indicate that on cutting there is no exudate, and the stems are hollow, while the blaze is recorded as "cream to green, longitudinal stripes, fibrous. Vascular rays obvious."

When it was first described in 1986 it was only known by a few collections from north-east of Chinchilla but with more recent attention because of its rarity, its known distribution has been considerably expanded. A further two populations have been found further south in the Goodiwindi area and there are a number of populations in the Theodore area to the north (Shapcott et al. 2017).
notes: Xerothamnella herbacea was included in a CSIRO report (Ponce Reyes et al. 2016) which provided costs for a prioritised set of threat management strategies for protecting the most threatened native plants and animals of the Queensland Brigalow Belt.

ecology_description: Grazed by native macropods and goats. Silcock (2014) recorded goats and macropods as grazing Xerothamnella parvifolia but although "often heavily browsed, occurred in abundance at sites close to water and with high dung counts, and substantial recruitment...was observed".
habitat_description: Locally common, at least in Queensland and South Australia, but is regarded as rare. Recorded from Gidgee (Acacia cambagei) low open woodland with a Senna understory in reddish clays with a gravel surface in Queensland, in light brown loams in Casuarina pauper open woodland over Senna artemisioides and Dodonaea microzyga in South Australia, and in the grazed area on Mount Poole (Jennings NSW221939) in New South Wales. For an account of the soil environment on Mount Poole see the website Environmental education for everyone - about soils. Silcock (2014) classified Xerothamnella parvifolia as a residual endemic species adapted to isolated residual habitat, in this case "Tertiary sandstone ranges (encompassing mesas, slopes, plateaus, toeslopes), and low hills and gibber plains of the Channel Country" of south-western Queensland, and with naturally few populations and a relatively restricted range.
distribution_description: Found in southern central Queensland, with disjunct occurrences in north-western New South Wales at Mount Poole, and the Gammon Ranges in the northern Flinders Range of South Australia. The South Australian occurrence was not documented until 1993 when it was first collected by Rick Davies from the Big Moro gorge region. There have been some recent findings (S.A. Arid Lands 2019) which have extended the range of the species in this area (Freckled Duck found in the Gammon Ranges).

ecology_description: Reproduces by seed and vegetatively via its short creeping stems (rhizomes). Has become a weed in parts of southern Australia, see Agapanthus praecox subsp. orientalis Weeds of Australia Fact Sheet (2016, accessed 3 October 2024).

distribution_description: Naturalised in southwestern Western Australia (Albany), southern and northern (e.g. near Tallangatta) Victoria, southeastern South Australia, New South Wales (e.g. Katoomba area, Blue Mountains), Lord Island Island and Tasmania. There are also records of established plants of uncertain status (possible remnant plantings, dumped garden refuse, plants at early stages of spreading and naturalising).
notes: A widely cultivated species; the plants clump quickly and propagate vegetatively as well as by seed. Recorded as persisting in old garden sites in Victoria by J.H. Willis, A Handbook to Plants in Victoria 1: 327 (1970), as Agapanthus orientalis. The leaves, rhizome and sap are reported to be poisonous; also a skin irritant (Shepherd 2004). Green (1994: 509) provides a treatment for Agapanthus on Lord Howe Island, where Agapanthus praecox subsp. orientalis is an escape from cultivation on the island and now seeding itself.
