fruit_description: Capsule broadly obloid, 6--11 mm long, 5--8 mm wide, or hemispherical with sepals reflexing and opening to c. 15 mm diam.
seed_description: seeds numerous, c. 0.8 mm long, reticulate
habitat_description: Common on samphire flats and saline areas inland.
distribution_description: Native to Europe and Africa; distributed widely throughout southern Australia.

habit_description: Semi-erect or prostrate, trailing, perennial subshrub to c. 40 cm high, minutely papillose
stem_description: Branches terete, appearing jointed from the persistent leaf-bases
leaf_description: Leaves terete, 4--15 mm long, c. 1 mm wide, opposite on lower branches, alternate on flowering branches, partly ensheathing stem, soon falling leaving only the broad base
inflorescence_description: pedicels 2--4 mm long (elongating in fruit) | peduncle 2--8 mm long
flower_description: Flowers solitary, terminal or axillary on short shoots | Sepals 5, 2--4 mm long, the outer 3 pointed and narrow, the inner obtuse and with broad membranous margins | Petal-like staminodes many, white or cream to very pale yellowish, shortly exceeding sepals | stamens many | Styles 5 | ovary inferior, locules 5, placentation axile
fruit_description: Capsule obovoid to globular, 2--4 mm diam. | valves winged along edges
seed_description: seeds many, D-shaped, laterally compressed, c. 0.8 mm long, minutely tuberculate, brown
distribution_description: Native to southern Africa. Naturalised mainly in south-eastern South Australia, western New South Wales and north-western Victoria; common along the Murray River in these states. There is also an adventive record (W.A. Low s.n., NT A0108643) from Alice Springs in the Northern Territory.
notes: This species resembles Mesembryanthemum in the form of the capsule and the alternate arrangement of the leaves on the flowering branchlets, but may be distinguished from other Australian representatives of the genus by the persistent leaf bases and minute papillae.

habit_description: Annual or biennial, decumbent to 1 m high
stem_description: Stems | vegetative stems and floral branches at least basally distinctly angled-ribbed
leaf_description: leaves, floral branches | Leaves opposite, decussate, petiolate, succulent, ovate-spathulate to lanceolate, (5.5-) 6--11 cm long, (1.8-) 3.5--4.5 (-5.5) cm wide, mid-green, paler on lower surface or reddish (exposed drier sites), with a slightly unpleasant scent | Floral leaves persistent
inflorescence_description: pedicels 20--30 mm long, receptacle 12--15 mm diam.
flower_description: flowers and fruit clothed in prominent succulent epidermal bladder cells, central stem erect with a leafy apex, 30--60 (-100) cm high, from which arise lateral floral branches in leaf axils, basal part of stem becoming somewhat woody up to 25 mm diam. | Flowers leaf-opposed | flowers (15-) 40--70 mm diam. | sepals unequal, outer 2--3 larger, triangular to oblong-ovate, triquetrous distally, lacking membranous margins | adaxial surface smooth, 9--12 mm long, the 2--3 inner smaller, similar in shape but with well-defined whitish membranous margins, 6--8 mm long | staminodes white, numerous, c. 180--220 exceeding sepals by 10--30 mm
fruit_description: Capsule (submature) hemispherical, 5--10-ribbed, 15--20 mm diam., succulent, red, prominently covered with epidermal bladder cells, glossy | mature capsules dehiscent, 10--15 mm diam., dry, straw-coloured
seed_description: seeds pale brown, triangular, c. 0.7--0.8 mm long, tuberculate
habitat_description: Readily invades degraded roadsides, forming dense, extensive stands, with some populations extending for kilometres along roadsides. Also frequently invades remnant roadside native vegetation along roadsides and adjacent private land, where it is a serious environmental weed. In contrast to M. crystallinum and M. nodiflorum which usually occur in inland and coastal areas, especially in Tecticornia-dominated habitats, M. guerichianum appears to prefer red brown sandy loam soils, appearing to avoid (at least for now) heavier soils.
distribution_description: Native to southern Africa. Naturalised west of c. Mildura in far south-western N.S.W. into far north-western Vic. and to near the border in far eastern S.A.

common_name: Small Ice-plant, Small Ice Plant, Slender Iceplant.
habit_description: Prostrate to weakly erect subshrub to 20 cm high, annual or biennial, densely papillose (glistening, bead-like papillae), often pink- to red-tinged
leaf_description: Leaves opposite at base, alternate on flowering branches, sessile, linear, semi-terete, flat on adaxial surface, 5--25 mm long, 1--2 mm wide, sparsely villous, papillose, soon withering
flower_description: Flowers mostly axillary, sessile or subsessile, 3--6 mm diam | Sepals 5, unequal, linear, subterete with a prominent horn (fleshy tubercle) at base, villous in lower half | Petal-like staminodes c. 4--5 mm long, white, sometimes yellowish or pink | Ovary faintly ribbed
fruit_description: Capsule obloid or obconic to narrowly ovoid, 4--8 mm long, 3--4 mm wide, the persistent sepals erect, not reflexed at maturity
seed_description: seeds numerous, to c. 1 mm long, reddish, tuberculate (faintly granular on one margin, fide Jessop 1986)
habitat_description: Common on samphire flats and saline areas inland.
distribution_description: Native to South Africa; distributed widely throughout southern Australia.

habit_description: Spreading to erect shrub
leaf_description: Leaves 3-angled, recurved, 10--36 mm long, 1--2 mm wide
inflorescence_description: peduncle 4--8 mm long
flower_description: Flowers pink, sometimes red or purplish
fruit_description: Capsule obconical to shallowly obconical, 2--4 mm long, 4--5 mm wide
habitat_description: Coastal sandy foreshores, sand dunes, rocky cliffs, road cutting near settlement.
distribution_description: Native of South Africa. Occasionally found along the coast near Adelaide, S.A., Melbourne, Vic., and Perth, W.A., but probably not always fully naturalised.
notes: See also Ruschia geminiflora in VICFLORA - Flora of Victoria (accessed 20 February 2025).

habit_description: Erect shrub to 10 cm
leaf_description: Leaves 25--50 mm long, 5--9 mm wide, dull green | the margins tinged pink | smooth, numerous pellucid dots evident beneath surface | adaxial surface flat | lateral surfaces convex
flower_description: keel smooth, sometimes denticulate on upturned portion | Flowers sessile or very shortly pedicellate, free (usually the first flowers) or shortly enclosed in fused bases of uppermost leaves | Styles 5, rarely 4 | ovary oblong, slightly compressed, acutely 2-keeled, slightly convex or nearly flat on top
distribution_description: Occurs in south-western W.A. (near coast south of Jurien Bay to Perth) and chiefly on Yorke Peninsula and Eyre Peninsula, S.A.

habit_description: Erect shrub to 30 cm
stem_description: branches angled | branchlets often tinged pink
leaf_description: Leaves acute or obtuse, 30--100 mm long, 4.5--7 mm wide, densely covered with small warts, glaucous with pink tinge at apex and along edges | adaxial surface flat | lateral surfaces convex
flower_description: keel either smooth or denticulate throughout | Flowers sessile or pedicellate, on branchlets at right angles to main stem, almost enclosed in a bilobed oblong involucre except petal-like staminodes | Sepals 4, rarely 5 | ovary oblong, terete, concave on top
habitat_description: Favouring sandy soils.
distribution_description: Widely distributed through southern Australia.

habit_description: Suberect herb
stem_description: stems to 1 m long, thick, smooth, nodes distant
leaf_description: Leaves linear, lanceolate or oblanceolate, connate at base, 10--70 mm long, 2--15 mm wide, smooth, fleshy, glossy green
inflorescence_description: Pedicels 3--15 mm long, thickening upwards
flower_description: Perianth tube 3 mm long | lobes triangular, 6--9 mm long, with scarious margins, with a distinct fleshy dorsal mucro behind apex c. 1.5 mm long, green outside, pink to purple inside | Stamens numerous | filaments c. 6 mm long | Ovary ovoid | styles 3, c. 4 mm long, locules 3 | ovules several per locule
fruit_description: Capsule operculum subovoid, c. 8 mm long, smooth
seed_description: Seeds several, pea-shaped to comma-shaped, c. 1.5 mm diam., smooth, black
habitat_description: Found on mudflats or in sand (e.g. beach foredunes and strandline), often associated with mangroves.
distribution_description: Occurs along the northern coast and islands of Australia.

habit_description: Annual herb with decumbent branches and sometimes also an erect central stem 0.05--0.2 m long, somewhat succulent
stem_description: Stems rather densely hairy at first but becoming sparsely hairy | the lower stems terete and up to 3 mm wide
leaf_description: Petioles absent or up to 25 mm long, densely hairy | Leaf blades ovate or broadly ovate with a long-attenuate base, 30--100 mm long, 15--50 mm wide, acute or obtuse | the margins flat | with papillae along the main veins and a dense pattern of circular impressions in between, often also with some papillae scattered over the surface, pale green or greyish green, with 2 or 3 prominent incurved lateral veins on each side of midvein
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence of solitary axillary flowers, each branch usually bearing 1--5 flowers or fruits spaced 10--40 mm apart | Pedicels 2--5 mm long
flower_description: Flowers yellow | Sepals (4) 5, ovate to broadly ovate, often unequal, 1.3--2 mm long, glabrous inside | Stamens more than twice as many as sepals | filament c. 1.5 mm long | anther c. 0.5 mm long | Ovary inferior, with short papillae on base and large ones at summit | Styles c. 7, c. 1.3 mm long
fruit_description: Fruit a diclesium, multicellular, greatly thickened and woody, obovoid or broadly obovoid and horned, 14--23 mm long including the horns, usually 10--15 mm wide, densely and conspicuously papillose | papillae mostly patent to reflexed, c. 1 mm long | horns 7--10, in a circle surrounding the truncate apex of fruit body, usually very unequal, most fairly straight and vertical but some curved or spreading, laterally compressed, triangular to broadly ovate-acuminate, the larger ones 4--9 mm long
seed_description: Seeds 1 per cell, c. 4 × 1.5 mm, pale brown
habitat_description: Recorded in reddish sandy soils or loam, sometimes associated with calcrete outcrops, on flat but not particularly low-lying ground, in vegetation dominated by Acacia; Acacia ramulosa scrub.
distribution_description: Occurs in the vicinity of Hamelin Station, near Shark Bay, Western Australia.

habit_description: Prostrate, annual, succulent herb, papillose on leaves and stems and with vesicular hairs on young growth
leaf_description: Leaves alternate, usually ovate or rhomboid, with midvein visible below. 1--5 cm long, 3--20 mm wide, narrowing to petiole 5--20 mm long, densely papillose or crystalline
flower_description: Flowers solitary, sessile | Perianth segments 4, lanceolate, c. 3 mm long, papillose outside, yellow inside | Stamens 12--20 | Ovary densely papillose | styles 3--8, filiform, c. 3 mm long
fruit_description: Fruit top-shaped, 15 mm long, 10 mm broad, densely papillose, purplish, bony, dry, usually with 4 wings extending above fruit but without horns, cuneate at base, with a number of convoluted ridges between wings
seed_description: Seeds 3--8, pear-shaped, pale brown
habitat_description: Grows in red sand, clay or rocky areas.
distribution_description: Occurs in the Meekatharra area, W.A.

habit_description: Decumbent or trailing undershrub with stout pale stems, densely papillose and with some vesicular hairs on young growth
leaf_description: Leaves thick, obovate, orbicular or oblong on lateral branches, with midvein and sometimes lateral veins visible below, 1--6 cm long, 5--30 mm wide, tapering to base, decurrent
inflorescence_description: pedicels 5--15 mm long, stout, papillose
flower_description: Flowers in groups of 3--5 in upper axils | Perianth segments 4, broadly ovate, 5 mm long, papillose outside, yellow inside | Stamens many, in 2 ranks | Ovary papillose | styles 4, stout, recurved, 2--3 mm long
fruit_description: Fruit dry, with 2 large and 2 smaller coriaceous or woody lateral wings alternating with small ridges, c. 10 mm long and 15 mm broad, papillose, pale
seed_description: Seeds 4, pear-shaped, c. 3 mm long, smooth, brown
habitat_description: Naturalised on coastal and estuarine sand dunes and on other coastal sites.
distribution_description: Introduced from southern Africa. Naturalised in coastal south-western W.A. (including Geraldton area south to Perth and Cape Leeuwin and records near Albany), near Adelaide, S.A., and recorded for central-coastal N.S.W. Also collected from Coode Island, Melbourne, Vic., between 1908 and 1912.

habit_description: Prostrate or semi-erect herb, branching from base, papillose but stems almost glabrous
leaf_description: Leaves lanceolate to rhomboid, 3--30 mm long, 2--10 mm wide, tapering to petiole up to 10 mm long
flower_description: Flowers solitary or occasionally paired, sessile, very small | Perianth segments 4, lanceolate, acute, c. 1 mm long, sparsely papillose | Stamens 4, alternating with perianth lobes | Ovary 4-angled | styles 4, 0.5 mm long
fruit_description: Fruit cuneate at base, heart-shaped, 5--8 mm long, 5--10 mm wide, with 2 thin membranous wings which are round at apex and extend above fruit
seed_description: Seeds 4, pear-shaped, c. 1.5 mm long, honey-coloured
habitat_description: Grows in sand and sandy loam, on sand dunes and outcropping limestone.
distribution_description: Occurs around Shark Bay south to Dalwallinu-Kalannie area, W.A.

habit_description: Prostrate annual, branching from base, papillose and with a few vesicular hairs
leaf_description: Leaves thick, succulent, lanceolate or rhomboid to ovate, 1--5 cm long, 4--15 mm wide, tapering to petiole 2--15 mm long
flower_description: Flowers solitary or occasionally paired, sessile or almost so | Perianth segments 4, ovate, 2 c. 1 mm long, 2 smaller, papillose outside towards apex, green inside | Stamens 4, alternating with perianth lobes | Ovary papillose | styles and locules 3--6, often 4
fruit_description: Fruit dry, compressed, c. 4 mm long, 4--8 mm diam., with 2 large and 2 smaller woody lateral triangular wings not extending above fruit, sometimes with 4 smaller ridges between wings
seed_description: Seeds 3--8, gourd- or pear-shaped, c. 2 mm long, honey-coloured
distribution_description: Widely distributed through central Australia, occasionally coastal. One specimen (MEL 522149) supposedly from the Snowy Mountains seems an error.

habit_description: Prostrate or sprawling herb with stout branches, papillose
leaf_description: Leaves lanceolate to oblanceolate with midvein visible below, 1--4.5 cm long, 2--10 mm wide, sessile
inflorescence_description: pedicels 4--15 mm long, papillose, elongating in fruit
flower_description: Flowers in groups of 2--5 in upper axils, occasionally single | Perianth segments 4, ovate, 3--4 mm long, papillose outside, yellow inside | Stamens many | Ovary papillose | styles and locules 3 or 4
fruit_description: Fruit with 4 large membranous wings rounded at apex and extending above fruit, cuneate at base, 8--25 mm long, 10--30 mm broad, becoming black
distribution_description: Introduced from southern Africa, collected twice in what is now suburban Melbourne but probably not naturalised.

common_name: Bower Spinach; also sometimes called Native Spinach or New Zealand Spinach, names used for Tetragonia tetragonoides.
habit_description: Prostrate or scrambling herb or subshrub, to 3 m long
leaf_description: Leaves alternate but often clustered, fleshy, papillose | petiole 3--15 mm long | lamina ovate-rhomboid to lanceolate to almost linear, 2--5 cm long
inflorescence_description: pedicels slender, 5--30 mm long
flower_description: Flowers solitary | Perianth lobes 4, oblong, c. 3 mm long, papillose-hairy outside, yellow inside | Stamens 12--20 | Ovary semi-inferior, locules and styles 2 (rarely 3)
fruit_description: Fruit subglobose, 5--8 mm long, red, succulent
habitat_description: Found usually on limestone and sand dunes. Common in coastal areas on Norfolk Island, for example on slopes in open forest (Green 1994).
distribution_description: Occurs along southern coasts from W.A. to Vic. and Tas.; also on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands.
notes: For treatment of Tetragonia implexicoma on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands see Green (1994).

profile_author: P.G. Kodela, S.W.L. Jacobs, J. Highet, A. Messina
flowers_per_inflorescence_description: Flowers paired or in clusters of up to 5
habit_description: Prostrate, spreading annual or, with branches to c. 50 cm long
leaf_description: Leaves alternate, trullate to angular-ovate or ovate to circular, (1-) 2--5 cm long, 5--25 mm wide, papillose, semi-succulent | petiole 5--20 mm long
flower_description: Flowers paired or in clusters of up to 5, 1--2 mm long, subsessile | perianth segments (3 or) 4, triangular, c. 1 mm long, green and smooth on inner surface, papillose on outer | stamens 4, alternating with, and usually as many as | perianth segments | styles 2 or 3
fruit_description: Fruit dry, obpyramidal, truncate or broadly convex on summit (with 3 or 4 projecting ridges forming flat triangular extensions at the top), c. 2--4 mm long, 3--4 angled, c. 3 mm diam.
seed_description: seeds 2 or 3, subgloboid, pale brown, 1.5--2 mm long
fire_response_description: At a Victorian site uncommon, germinated post-fire (Walsh 9123, MEL n.v.)
germination_description: At a Victorian site uncommon, germinated post-fire (Walsh 9123, MEL n.v.)
ecology_description: At a Victorian site uncommon, germinated post-fire (Walsh 9123, MEL n.v.).
distribution_description: Native of southern Africa. In Australia, collected from a few localities in N.S.W. and Vic. Known in Vic. from a 1970 collection from the Snowy River near the New South Wales border at Willis, and more recently a 2021 collection from the Snowy River.

description_treatment_used: current FoA text (after earlier cited treatments)
habit_description: Prostrate or decumbent annual with branches to c. 50 cm long
leaf_description: Leaves usually narrowly to broadly ovate, elliptic or rhombic, 2--10 cm long, 0.6--5 cm wide, papillose, succulent | petiole 0.6--2 cm long
flower_description: Flowers solitary, sessile or subsessile | perianth segments 4, unequal, triangular or broadly triangular, 1--2 mm long, green and smooth on inner surface | outer surface densely papillose | stamens 4--8 | styles mostly 8--13
fruit_description: Fruit dry or thinly succulent, laterally compressed, broadly ovoid to ellipsoid, 6--14 mm long and wide, variously ribbed, with 2 prominent incurved | claw-like projections and 2--6 smaller projections, or with 4 equal projections
seed_description: seeds mostly 8--13, asymmetrically ovoid, pale brown, c. 2.5 mm long
habitat_description: Sand dunes and swales, light-and heavy-textured soils from red sands to grey cracking clays, particularly in areas subject to periodic inundation (e.g. floodplains, creek and stream banks, gilgais, claypans).
distribution_description: Occurs in arid and semi-arid areas of Western Australia, South Australia, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria (Fig. 2 in Gray 1997: 121). The species could possibly occur in the Northern Territory portion of the Simpson Desert.

habit_description: Soft, prostrate, slightly succulent herb with underground tuber, much branched, glabrous or papillose or with hair-like scales, green or purplish, drying black
leaf_description: Leaves broadly ovate to orbicular, 1--8 cm long, 6--35 mm wide | upper leaves narrower, narrowing to petiole 5--30 mm long
inflorescence_description: pedicels 5--25 mm long, papillose
flower_description: Flowers grouped | Perianth segments 4 or 5, ovate, acute, c. 3 mm long, papillose or hairy, green | Stamens many | Styles and locules 3 or 4
fruit_description: Fruit dry, with 4 thin smooth wings, 5--15 mm long, indented at apex, slightly narrowed at base
distribution_description: Introduced from southern Africa. Recorded as naturalised from a site in Perth, W.A.

common_name: New Zealand Spinach, Native Spinach, Warrigal Greens, Warrigal Cabbage, Botany Bay Greens.
description_treatment_used: current FoA text (after earlier cited treatments)
habit_description: Prostrate or sprawling annual with branches to c. 1 m. long
leaf_description: Leaves deltoid to rhombic, 2--8 cm long, 1--5 cm wide, prominently papillose, succulent | petiole 1--3 cm long
flower_description: Flowers solitary, sessile or subsessile | perianth segments 5, unequal, acute to obtuse, c. 2 mm long, green on inner surface, densely papillose on outer | stamens 10--16 | styles 5--11
fruit_description: Fruit dry or thinly succulent, prominently papillose when fresh, turbinate, c. 1 cm long and wide, prominently 4-angled or winged, sometimes with 2 smaller angles, main angles terminating in short conical horns
seed_description: seeds usually 4--8, narrowly ovoid, pale brown, 2--3 mm long
habitat_description: Usually in coastal areas, often in sand or peaty sand or growing in rock crevices; coastal cliffs, coastal lake shores/saline estuaries, base of beach dunes, beaches, river banks. Also occurs further inland in heavier soils and near rivers and salt lakes; recorded in rainforest, eucalypt woodland, creek bed in seasonal wetland in riparian open forest, and Brigalow scrub in Qld. On Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands a native of coastal cliffs, stabilised sand and similar habitats near the sea (Green 1994: 79).
distribution_description: Native to Australia, New Zealand and according to Plants of the World (accessed 24 February 2025) southern China to Vietnam and temperate eastern Asia, and Australasia to New Caledonia; naturalised in many parts of the world including the Americas, Africa and Europe. Found in coastal and some further inland areas of southern Australia (SW W.A., SE S.A. to SE Qld); see Figure 2 in Gray (1997: 121).
notes: Adventitious buds occasionally develop from the persistent calyx and produce new small flowers which are sometimes fertile. For treatment of Tetragonia tetragonoides on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands see Green (1994). The history of both Tetragonia moorei and T. tetragonioides as potential stock poisons, medicinal plants and human food is briefly discussed by Gray (1997). An agricultural weed in parts of Queensland.

habit_description: Small, prostrate or ascending herb, much-branched, glabrous
leaf_description: Leaves oblong to orbicular, 4--7 mm long and wide, the larger of each opposite pair petiolate with a large denticulate hemispherical sheath at base, the smaller a lamina and sheath only
inflorescence_description: pedicels 2--4 mm long | bract 1, ovate
flower_description: Flowers solitary | Perianth tube c. 1.5 mm long | lobes semi-ovate, c. 2 mm long, pink inside | Stamens 5--7, irregularly arranged | filaments c. 1.5 mm long | Ovary globular | style thick, c. 0.5 mm long | ovules many
fruit_description: Capsule operculum subglobular, c. 2 mm long, thin
seed_description: Seeds several, triangular to reniform, c. 0.5 mm long, very shiny, black, smooth
distribution_description: Occurs around the shores of the Gulf of Carpentaria, N.T. and Qld

habit_description: Prostrate, slender, small herb, glabrous
leaf_description: Leaves obovate or orbicular, c. 5 mm long | petiole slender, dilated at base with scarious margins
inflorescence_description: bracts scarious
flower_description: Flowers in loose cymes exceeding leaves | Perianth tube short | lobes broad, obtuse, c. 2 mm long | Stamens 7--10 | Ovary short, rounded | style slightly excentric, terminal, linear, recurved | ovules 6--12
fruit_description: Fruit globular
seed_description: Seeds smooth
distribution_description: Known only from the type, collected in N.S.W.
notes: This description has been taken from G.Bentham, Fl. Austral. 3: 331 (1867). Not listed by S.W.L. Jacobs & J. Pickard, Pl. New South Wales (1981). The record by F.M. Bailey, Compr. Cat. Queensland Pl. (1913), was a misapplication of the name to T. compacta.

habit_description: Prostrate herb, much-branched, glabrous
leaf_description: Leaves ovate or obovate, thick, acute, cuneate at base, 3--15 mm long, 3--10 mm wide | petiole 5--6 mm long | sheath scarious, with acute lobes
inflorescence_description: pedicels 3--5 mm long | bracts 2, lanceolate, denticulate, apiculate, as long as pedicel
flower_description: Flowers solitary | Perianth tube very short | lobes c. 6 mm long, very unequal, the outer lanceolate-oblong, the inner broadly oval, with scarious edges, rarely with minute dorsal mucro, abruptly spreading, pink inside | Stamens 15--25 | filaments c. 4 mm long | Ovary glabrous | style flattened, recurved, c. 1 mm long | ovules c. 10
fruit_description: Fruit dehiscing near middle | Capsule operculum subovoid, c. 4 mm long, papery
seed_description: Seeds 4--8, pear-shaped, c. 1 mm long, shiny, black, longitudinally furrowed along dorsal edge
distribution_description: Scattered through the northern half of W.A. and occasionally collected in N.T.

habit_description: Much-branched, prostrate, annual herb c. 20 cm in diam. and 5 cm high, glabrous
stem_description: the branches here or unequal diam
leaf_description: Leaves opposite, flat, elliptic to obovate, 4--11 mm long and 1.5--5 mm wide, often with a short mucro at apex, basally shortly connate, weakly papillose, succulent due to the large water-storing cells of the epidermis and hypodermis, reddish on abaxial surface, leaves in the flowering region anisophyllous, with the thicker side branch in the axil or the larger leaf | petiole 1--2 mm long, basally expanded into a membranaceous sheath with 2 acuminate lobes
inflorescence_description: pedicels to 2 mm long at anthesis, but elongated up to 5 mm when fruiting, with 2 scarious, lanceolate, apiculate and denticulate bracts
flower_description: Flowers solitary, axillary, with an intense honey smell at anthesis | perianth c. 7.5 mm in diam., 5-partite | tube obconical, c. 2 mm long, with a whitish nectary disc inside at base | lobes green outside, whitish pink inside, valvate | stamens 10, 5 opposite and 5 alternate to the tepals, inserted at the mouth of the perianth tube | anthers pale pink, smooth | style 1, filiform with a row of short papillae on one side | placenta marginal with 10--12 ovules in 2 rows | operculum subovoid
fruit_description: Capsule dehiscing by circumscissile split about the middle
seed_description: seeds 6--8, broadly ovoid or pyriform, c . 1.1 × 0.9 × 0.6 mm, brownish to black, smooth, completely sheathed by an aril, which swells slightly when moistened | embryo horseshoe-shaped, curved around the mealy perisperm
habitat_description: Grows on flat hills in schistose rock.
distribution_description: Only known from type locality in the southern Kimberley region, Western Australia.

habit_description: Prostrate perennial herb
stem_description: stems to 1 m long, densely hairy
leaf_description: Leaves ovate to obovate or spathulate, acute or obtuse | lamina 3--30 mm long, 3--15 mm wide, light green, paler below | petiole c. 6 mm long, sometimes dilated into a membranous sheath
inflorescence_description: pedicels 2--10 mm long | bracts lanceolate, inconspicuous
flower_description: Flowers solitary | Perianth tube 1--2 mm long, abruptly dilated | lobes spreading, narrowly triangular, c. 6 mm long, white to pink inside with mauve tips | Stamens 5--15 | filaments 3--4 mm long | Ovary cylindrical | style recurved, c. 2.5 mm long | ovules 2
fruit_description: Capsule operculum campanulate with undulating rim, 2--3 mm broad, membranous
seed_description: Seed 1, compressed pea-shaped, c. 3 mm broad, reticulate or rugose, studded with small clear papillae, black, tightly enclosed in operculum
habitat_description: Found in sandy soils.
distribution_description: Occurs in northern N.T. around Oenpelli, Jabiru and Jim Jim Falls.

habit_description: Prostrate or ascending herb, glabrous or young stems sparsely hirsute
leaf_description: Leaves lanceolate, ovate, obovate or spathulate | lamina 3--25 mm long, 1--8 mm wide | petiole 3--8 mm long, abruptly expanded into an oblong sheath with acuminate lobes
inflorescence_description: bracts linear-lanceolate, apiculate
flower_description: Flowers larger than leaves, in threes, occasionally paired or solitary, sessile or on pedicels to 10 mm long | Perianth tube obconical, 2--3 mm long | lobes lanceolate-oblong to ovate, 5--6 mm long | Stamens 10--20, free | Ovary ovoid | style filiform, c. 2.5 mm long, recurved | ovules 10--12
fruit_description: Fruit dehiscing about middle, c. 6 mm long | Capsule operculum subovoid, tapering into slender persistent style
seed_description: Seeds 6--9, comma-shaped, 2 mm wide including papillae, black
distribution_description: Occurs in northern Western Australia and central Northern Territory.
notes: There are 2 varieties.

flower_description: Flowers distinctly pedicellate | Staminal filaments flared at base
seed_description: Seeds studded with elongate papillae increasing in size towards the back to 0.2 mm long

ecology_description: Hydrocleys nymphoides is stoloniferous and spreads locally by its creeping stems. In the absence of seeds, the probable mode of wider dispersal would involve stem fragments and small plantlets (produced at the end of the growing season); these apomicts break off and float away to take root in a suitable location. Dispersal vectors are most likely to be water currents, machinery, boats, water fowl, and people.

distribution_description: Native to S America, from Venezuela to Brazil and S to Buenos Aires, Argentina. Naturalised in Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria; also recorded for Norfolk Island.
notes: For a history of Hydrocleys nymphoides in Australia see Aston & Jacobs (1980) and Kodela & Jobson (2018). There are no records of fruit in the Australian populations, suggesting the possibility it may represent a single clone, or other factors required for fertilisation and seed set are absent (Aston & Jacobs 1980, Kodela & Jobson 2018). However, Hydrocleys nymphoides can reproduce and spread vegetatively, and has the potential to be an invasive weed, particularly in disturbed wetlands and waterways (Aston & Jacobs 1980, Richardson et al. 2011, Romanowski 2011, Randall 2017, Mifsud 2018, Agriculture Victoria 2019, Kodela & Jobson 2018).

notes: The leek, Allium porrum L., known only in cultivation, is a cultigen derived from A. ampeloprasum, which it resembles in flower, but differs in its biennial life-cycle, stout cylindrical bulb, much broader leaves and much less pungent taste. It may survive for a short period as a relic of previous cultivation, and is known as an occasional escape on disturbed sites in metropolitan Perth, Western Australia (Osborne Park, 20 Dec. 1952, collector unknown, PERTH). Variants of A. ampeloprasum with bulbils in the umbel have been recognised in W Europe but are not known to occur in Australia.

habit_description: Plant with odour of garlic when crushed

notes: Also reported as a weed of cultivation in southeastern Qld (Kleinschmidt & Johnson 1977: 136, as N. inodorum), the A.C.T. (Burbidge & Gray 1970: 108, as N. inodorum) and the western districts of Vic. (Willis 1962: 1: 325, as N. inodorum).

habit_description: Tufted perennial herb with rhizome and fibrous roots
leaf_description: Leaves linear, grey-green to bluish, garlic/onion-scented, shorter than inflorescence

habit_description: Shrub, 1.5--4 m
leaf_description: Leaves often in whorls of 3 or 4, obovate-oblong to oblanceolate, 5--35 cm long, 2--6 cm wide, cuneate, tapering into the 3--25 mm long petiole | base attenuate | margin entire | apex obtuse-acuminate | venation faint on both surfaces | the midrib slightly sulcate | slightly prominent abaxially

habitat_description: An understory shrub in tropical closed forests (well-developed upland and mountain rainforest), often on soils derived from granite; 100--1250 m alt.
distribution_description: North Queensland in Bellenden-Ker Range and slopes of the Atherton Tableland and Daintree Wilderness.
seedling_description: Cotyledons 3 (), broadly spathulate, c. 10 mm long, 6 mm wide, margins sparsely toothed, First pair of leaves: shortly petiolate. Tenth leaf stage: leaves shortly petiolate, apex mucronate, base attenuate, lateral veins not apparent. Cataphylls intermingled with the true leaves. Petioles somewhat decurrent on the stems. Indumentum of dark reddish brown hairs usually visible in the leaf axils.
notes: The flowers are heavily and sweetly perfumed. L.S.Smith (14683) noted that the base of the lower branches is often decumbent and rooting.

common_name: Peruvian Lily, Alstroemeria, Yellow Alstroemeria, Golden-flowered Alstroemeria, Lily of the Incas, Golden Peruvian Lily, Yellow Peruvian Lily, Chilean Lily.
habit_description: Herb with many simple stems to 1.2 m long from thin rhizome, with tuberous roots

seed_description: Seeds rugose-tuberculate, 2--3 mm diam., reddish brown

distribution_description: A Chilean species naturalised in the ranges north and east of Melbourne (see Conran 1994), Victoria; sparingly naturalised in the Southern Tablelands of New South Wales (Wilson 2017), and in Tasmania (Baker et al. 2019: 60). Adventive plants have also been sparingly recorded from the Adelaide Hills, South Australia.
notes: The naturalised population at Mount Macedon covers several hectares. All parts of plant cause skin allergies (Shepherd 2004).

habit_description: Herb with many simple stems to 1 m long from thin rhizome, with fleshy tuberous roots

fruit_description: Capsule angularly subglobose with prominent ribs, 1--1.5 cm diam
seed_description: Seeds rugose-tuberculate, 2.5--3 mm diam., reddish brown
habitat_description: Grows in shady areas, in disturbed sites usually near settlement and with other weeds; recorded from weedy creek banks, riparian vegetation, wetlands, edges of rainforest, tall open eucalypt forest, eucalypt woodland, a damp paddock, an artificial ditch, footpath, roadsides and embankments.
distribution_description: Native to South America (southern Brazil, northern Argentina, northeastern Paraguay). In Australia, an escape from cultivation, naturalised in southwestern Western Australia, southeastern Queensland, coastal New South Wales, and sparingly in Victoria; also on Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands.
notes: Occurs as a garden escape that can become an environmental weed. Reported to be naturalised in Dandenong Ranges, southern Victoria, (J.H. Willis, Handb. Pl. Victoria 1: 327, 1970), but no specimens seen. For an account of Alstroemeria psittacina on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands see Green (1994), as A. pulchella.

habit_description: Tree to 9 m high, soft-wooded

ecology_description: A canopy-gap plant requiring an opening in the forest canopy to successfully establish. Established seedlings on valley floors can be washed away by heavy rain, while the vine Ipomoea cairica can smother young and adult plants.
habitat_description: The few natural occurrences on Norfolk Island suggest that this species favours streamside and damp forest situations. Can grow in the shade of Norfolk Palm (Rhopalostylis baueri), occasionally on ridges but most commonly in gullies on valley floors or lower valley sides (Director of National Parks 2010: 77).
distribution_description: Endemic to Norfolk Island; now confined to small populations in a few forested valleys.
notes: Achyranthes arborescens, along with A. mangarevica Suess. (from Mangareva Islands, Polynesia) and A. margaretarum de Lange (from Phillip Island), which are not quite as tall, are the only truly arborescent members of the family.

distribution_description: Pantropical. In Australia, a widespread native that grows throughout northern Australia from Derby in Western Australia, south to Alice Springs, Northern Territory, in central Australia and to the Queensland/New South Wales border and Barrier Reef islands. Some specimens were collected from the Sydney region pre-1930. Also on Christmas Island, Cocos Keeling Islands, Coral Sea Islands, Norfolk Island and Lord Howe Island.
notes: Treatment for Achyranthes aspera L. on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands provided by Green (1994: 88); for Christmas, Cocos (Keeling) and Coral Sea Islands see Barker & Telford (1993: 115).

common_name: Pig’s Knee, Achyranthes Root, Ox Knee.

habit_description: Shrub to 2 (-3) m high, soft-wooded, much-branched, compact

fruiting_time_description: Flowers and fruits February-November, but mainly April-September
habit_description: Herb, perennial, erect to spreading, to 150 cm high, dioecious

distribution_description: Widespread in the drier parts of the tropics and subtropics from western Africa across the Middle East to Burma. It occurs in northern Western Australia in the Kimberley, south to Carnarvon and inland to Wittenoom Gorge; in the Victoria River district and a few other scattered localities in the Northern Territory; Oodnadatta in South Australia; scattered occurrences in north-western Queensland mostly around Cloncurry and further south near Roma; and in the interior of New South Wales.
notes: Aerva javanica is thought to have been accidentally introduced in the 1880s probably in fodder and saddle packs for the Afghan camel trains. Along with Buffel and Birdwood Grasses (Cenchrus spp.) it was later deliberately introduced to the Ord River catchment area in north-western Western Australia to aid in regeneration of overgrazed and water-eroded areas. It has since also proved to be a useful fodder plant for cattle during drought. Being a prolific seeder it has spread across northern Australia by various means, one being as seed contamination of Buffel Grass introductions.

habitat_description: Grows in a variety of habitats: in skeletal soils in open woodland or grassland on plateaux, rocky ridges and slopes of sandstone, limestone, granite or basalt; in red sandy lateritic soils or pure sand to sandy clays in Eucalyptus and or Acacia open woodland or scrub with Spinifex, Sorghum and other grasses on undulating hills, plains and river terraces; on coastal sand dunes in sheltered areas; on disturbed areas (along roadsides).
distribution_description: Widespread and common in the Pilbara and Kimberley regions of Western Australia; in the Northern Territory from Cobourg Peninsula in the north, south to Tennant Creek, across the Barkly Tableland and the Gulf east to Normanton in Queensland. Also extends into Timor and the Moluccas. One collection from Uluru National Park in the south of the Northern Territory is probably the result of an introduction by travellers.

habitat_description: Gomphrena celosoides is a common weed of disturbed areas, mown lawns and grasslands, mostly in sandy or heavy brown soils.
distribution_description: Native in South America, this species has become a weed in the tropical and subtropical parts of the world including Australia. It occurs in Western Australia at Port Hedland, on the Dampier Peninsula and around Kununurra in the Kimberley; scattered through northern and central Northern Territory and is most widespread in eastern Australia from the islands off Cape York in Queensland to Nowra in southern New South Wales and inland to west of Cunnamulla. It has also been recorded from southern South Australia, and occurs on Christmas Island.
notes: A treatment for Gomphrena celosioides on Christmas Island is provided by Barker in Barker & Telford (1993: 118). Horses may be poisoned if confined to areas with large amounts of this species but little other fodder, suffering from ‘Coastal Staggers’ (Everist 1974: 57).

notes: Bentham (1870) cites a specimen collected by Bynoe of this species from the Victoria River in the Northern Territory (K 000357258). This specimen is Gomphrena conferta but as there are no other collections from this area, the occurrence of this species in the Northern Territory requires confirming.

notes: The small hooks on the tepals have presumably evolved as an aid to seed dispersal.

Widespread in the tropics of the Old World, throughout Africa and east across Asia, India, Malaya, Philippines, Papua New Guinea (Indomalaysia, Paupuasia, Africa).
notes: Probably introduced, as all localities are near the coast and most records are over 20 years old.

habit_description: Herb, erect to trailing, annual to perennial, to 1.5 m high

fruit_description: Fruit ellipsoidal, c. 2.5 mm long
seed_description: Seed ellipsoidal to circular, (1.6-) 1.8--2 mm long
habitat_description: Occurs in disturbed areas such as edges of vine thickets and monsoon woodlands on sands, limestone, granite and laterites.
distribution_description: Widespread in eastern central Africa, presumably introduced in Asia and Australia. Occurs on the Dampier Peninsula, Port Warrender, and Prince Frederick Harbour in Western Australia; Daly River Reserve area, around Katherine and Murgenella in Northern Territory; Palmer River area in north Queensland. Normanby River, V.J. Neldner 3821 (DNA)' determined as Pupalia micrantha - Editor.]
notes: This species seems to have arrived in Australia fairly recently, with the earliest collection from near Katherine in 1965. The majority of specimens are from coastal regions of northern Western Australia and Northern Territory. There is a immature specimen collection from Queensland (J.R. Clarkson 6704 & W.F. McDonald) and V.J. Neldner 3821 requiring further investigation. The rest are inland near Katherine. The majority of specimens for this genus in Australia are referred to this taxon and not P. lappacea.

flowering_time_description: Flowers November-July; fruits persistent into next flowering season

phenology_text: Flowers November-July; fruits persistent into next flowering season.
habitat_description: Grows with samphire spp. on coastal saltmarshes and mangrove swamps and also on limestone cliffs in South Australia. In inland areas it grows on salt-pan and lake margins in sandy gypseous soils.
distribution_description: Occurs along the northwest coast of Western Australia from Dampierland Peninsula S to Shark Bay and inland; throughout coastal and inland South Australia; central Northern Territory; and one record from NW Victoria.

flowering_time_description: Flowers January-June; fruits persist into next flowering season
habit_description: Shrub, erect, bushy, 50--150 cm high, up to 150 cm diam.

notes: Sap and bulb poisonous; also a skin irritant (Shepherd 2004; 45).

notes: Possibly only a colour variant of Calostemma purpureum, though mostly larger in its parts.

pollination_description: The flowers open in the evening and are pollinated by a hawk moth, recorded by H.N. Ridley (loc. cit.), as Sphinx convolvuli (Agrius convolvuli (Linnaeus 1758)) on Christmas Island
ecology_description: The flowers open in the evening and are pollinated by a hawk moth, recorded by H.N. Ridley (loc. cit.), as Sphinx convolvuli (Agrius convolvuli (Linnaeus 1758)) on Christmas Island. The erect inflorescences often deposit their seed higher up the cliff than the parent plant, leading to a slow ascent up the cliffs. The inland cliffs on Christmas Island must have been first colonised when they were at sea level, and have maintained their populations since.
habitat_description: H.N. Ridley, Journal of the Straits Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society 45: 236 (1906), recorded it as common on Christmas Island in Flying Fish Cove and on rocks and cliffs throughout. It has been removed from most readily accessible situations for cultivation in gardens but is still quite frequent on exposed cliffs, both at the coast and on the tiers of inland cliffs. It grows in partially shady to very exposed situations, on ledges and in crevices in the limestone. On Cocos (Keeling) Islands grows in coralline sand at the top of beaches, or in gullies or depressions.
distribution_description: Occurs on Christmas Island and Cocos (Keeling) Islands. A widespread species, distributed from Sri Lanka and India to S China and Japan, through Indo-China, Malesia, the Philippines to the Pacific islands.

habit_description: Glabrous geophytic perennial, with a bulb that is often extended as a neck to ground level
leaf_description: Leaves 6--8, basal, sessile, deciduous, erect, 340--690 mm long, 5.1--11.7 mm wide, dull green to slightly glaucous, with parallel venation, not obviously keeled, with a lunate (U-shaped) channel 5.5--10.7 mm deep | base to 20 mm wide where flaring | thickly spongy-succulent | margin sparsely but distinctly tuberculate along most of length | apex acute

flower_description: Flower buds pendulous, yellowish cream externally just before anthesis, c. 60 mm long, 10--18 mm diam., narrowly obovoid, acute | Flowers sessile, bright white inside and out at anthesis, suffused with pink then maroon to dark purple with age (or rapidly after picking), sweetly scented, with a slender tube and spreading tepal lobes | tube 85--120 mm long, c. 5 mm diam. at base, 4.0--4.5 mm diam. in middle, 3--4 mm diam. at apex, cylindrical but slightly tapering to apex, smooth but becoming very shallowly and broadly grooved near apex, nectar-filled, with an abscission ring present at base at maturity | outer corolla lobes narrowly elliptic to narrowly obovate or oblanceolate, 62--87 mm long, 11--18 mm wide (shrinking to c. 12 mm wide on wilting) | apex attenuate | Anthers greenish yellow, aging dark brown to black, 8.5--11.7 mm long, allantoid, medifixed, latrorse, turning inside out and frequently curving after anthesis | pollen yellow to orange | Ovary 3-locular, inferior, broadly spindle-shaped, green, 10--12 mm long, 6--7 mm diam., on a thick gynophore 2--4 mm long (sometimes appearing almost sessile), ovary beak absent | ovules c. 10 per loculus, in 2 rows | Style filiform, pinkish red to maroon, sometimes white in basal ½, exceeding stamens, 132--162 mm long, 0.7--0.9 mm diam., exceeding corolla tube by 67--72 mm, smooth, usually declinate | stigma shortly 2- or 3-lobed or sub-capitate, c. 1.3--2.2 mm diam., with a dense cluster of repeatedly dividing papillae
fruit_description: Fruit globular or irregular, 30--40 mm diam
seed_description: Seeds 1-several, 7--10 mm across, irregular to subglobular
habitat_description: Grows on seasonally wet sand flats on sandstone and in shallow, flooded soils over basalt. Recorded in association with Alloteropsis semialata, Cochlospermum fraseri, Corymbia spp., Decaschistia occidentalis, Erythrophleum chlorostachys, Ipomoea sp., Owenia vernicosa, Terminalia canescens and Triodia spp.

Recorded in W.A. from a swamp and paddock.

common_name: Swamp Lily, River Lily, Spider Lily, Murray Lily.
habit_description: Plant robust with a pseudostem up to 45 cm high

distribution_description: Native in coastal swamps and on river banks, on Wessel Is., N.T., along the coast and offshore islands in Qld and in N.S.W. south to Jervis Bay. Also on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands, and in New Guinea. J.G. Baker (Handbook of the Amaryllideae 77, 1888) recorded it for New Caledonia, Fiji and Timor.
notes: Characterised by the robust pseudostem, large broad leaves with entire margins, large inflorescence arising in leaf axil and pedicellate flowers with narrow decurving perianth lobes and long straight anthers. Although the name Crinum asiaticum L. has been misapplied to C. angustifolium in Australia, C. asiaticum appears to be more closely related to C. pedunculatum. The delimitation between these two species needs further investigation. Particular attention should be paid to ovule number. For treatment of Crinum pedunculatum on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands see Green (1994: 509--510), as Crinum asiaticum L. var. pedunculatum (R.Br.) Fosberg & Sachet.

ecology_description: There is a record of a large number of seedlings in partial to deep shade beneath Alstonia scholaris, Acacia and Corymbia sp. where the nearest adult plant is unknown but it is thought to have been dispersed to the site by rats or cockatoos (viz. B.M. Waterhouse 6846; BRI). Also possibly dispersed by fruit bats (viz. B.M. Waterhouse 4285; BRI, MEL). Has potential to become a serious environmental weed locally, e.g. on Horn Island where seedlings and saplings are clustered and often abundant beneath trees which provide perching or roosting sites for fruit bats and cockatoos (viz. B.M. Waterhouse 2999, 5339; BRI). Pollination biology of cashew, including insects visiting the flowers, has been investigated in the Northern Territory; see Heard et al. (1990).

ecology_description: Widespread in northern Australia with most occurrences a result from human activities but the seeds are also spread by other vectors. The fallen fruit is eaten by cattle, and horses will spit the seeds out. Fruiting attracts Fruit Bats/Flying Foxes (Pteropus spp.). (Zich et al. 2018). The disseminule has been recorded as flotsam on Ashmore Reef islands, and is described and illustrated by Pike & Leach (1997: 126, 138). A diversity of insects visit mango flowers, including many species of bees, wasps, flies, beetles, ants and butterflies. Studies suggest that flies are important in mango pollination. As pollinators for economic crops such as mangos, flies are likely to represent a good alternative or supplemental option to bees because different species are present all year round and frequently visit flowers to feed on nectar and/or pollen to support key biological functions including flight and reproduction. (Cook et al. 2020); see Cook et al. (2020), and references therein, for details.
habitat_description: Recorded naturalised in rainforest, gallery forest, riparian woodland, open eucalypt forest, on old farmland, often near streams.
distribution_description: Originally from Indo-Burma region. Cultivated in Australia and occasionally naturalised in northern Western Australia, northern Northern Territory, scattered along the eastern coast of Queensland from Cape York Peninsula and Torres Strait islands to northeastern New South Wales.
notes: A variable species.

distribution_description: Naturalised on Christmas Island. Introduced as a fruit tree, and old trees often mark areas previously cultivated. It is now quite common on the island, and many specimens are self-sown. The natural distribution of Mangifera ×odorata has been obscured through its widespread cultivation throughout Malesia, but it occurs in lowland forest in Sumatra, Java and Borneo.
notes: A second species of mango, Mangifera indica L., is also cultivated on Christmas Island. This species is probably native to India and Burma, but is widely cultivated throughout the tropics, and is commercially the most important mango. The seed produced on Christmas Island is viable and seedlings will grow freely if the fruit is not collected, suggesting that this species may become naturalised in the future. The fruit is delicious eaten raw or dried, and may be used to make pickles, chutney or jam. It is most easily distinguished from M. ×odorata by its more slender, glossy leaves with an undulating margin, its shortly hairy inflorescence, its broader, papillose disc and its more brightly coloured fruit; D.A. Powell 659 (K).

notes: This species shows strong heterophylly, with remarkable variation in size, form and pigmentation of leaf laminas. Much of the variation is ontogenetic and consistent: early juvenile plants climb or creep exclusively by clinging roots and have very small laminas that are purple beneath; intermediate (late-juvenile) plants have large, thin, cordate, green leaves, while adult, flowering plants have small to medium-sized, tough, thick, non-cordate, green laminas and lack clinging roots. notes: Parsonsia velutina has the widest range in Australia of any Parsonsia and shows marked variation in leaf size, indumentum and inflorescence morphology. The variation is in part geographical and may, with further study, allow recognition or reinstatement of two or more distinct taxa. The species, as here circumscribed, is distinguished by the usually medium-sized to large, ovate or oblong-ovate leaves, the usual presence of a dense, soft, fawn to brown tomentum on the laminas, and the consistently cordate lamina base, by the small flowers that are subsessile and in dense, discrete clusters within the panicle, by the corolla with erect lobes which enclose the anther cone, and by the spreading sepals. Populations from New South Wales and southern Queensland have short peduncles 0.2--3 cm long, while the northern Australian specimens have much longer peduncles to 13 cm long, and usually have the bifurcation or trifurcation at the peduncle apex well-developed. The leaf indumentum shows much variation. Within one region different populations may be softly fawn-pubescent, densely rusty-pubescent or glabrescent to almost glabrous.
